The Council's projection for global import demand is trimmed fractionally m/m, to 190m t, still representing an all-time peak. Expectations for world rice supply and demand in 2025/26 are broadly unchanged m/m, with a modest 0.5m t reduction in trade mostly tied to a downgraded import figure for the Philippines. Global output in 2026/27 is projected steady m/m and down by 11m t y/y (year-on-year). With consumption predicted to gain, combined inventories are set to tighten. Trade in 2027 is seen little-changed at a record of 61m t. World grains and oilseeds export markets had a softer tone during the past month, but rice values were firmer. Overall, the IGC Grains and Oilseeds Index (GOI) was down by 4%. (see chart) (see chart) (see chart) World total grains production in 2026/27 is expected to be 68m t lower y/y at 2,427m. The decline includes 40m t of maize and 25m of wheat, while barley is seen 4m higher. Grains consumption is forecast to be up marginally to a new high of 2,446m t, with increased food and industrial uptake just about offsetting reduced feeding. Even after this month's increase, end-season stocks are still predicted to tighten, placed 19m t down y/y, at 619m. World trade (Jul/Jun) is projected to reach 450m t, a drop of 17m, including notable falls in wheat (-15m) and barley (-7m), but an increase for maize (+6m). Chiefly due to an anticipated record US outturn, together with potentially sizeable South American crops, world soyabean output in 2026/27 is forecast at a peak (+2%). With growing demand for soya derivatives set to underpin further gains in consumption, aggregate carryovers are predicted to tighten, including a reduction in exporters' reserves. Given tentative expectations for ample and attractively priced surpluses at key origins, trade could expand by 2% y/y to a fresh high, led by firmer Asian buying interest. (see chart) Projected to contract for the first time in more than 10 years, global rice production in 2026/27 is pegged at 536m t (-2%) including a 6m decline in India. Expanding food requirements in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia are likely to underpin a 1% increase in consumption, while combined reserves could decrease for the first time in four years, albeit staying historically comfortable. Trade in 2027 is predicted at a peak, boosted by potentially firmer demand from African buyers. (see chart) After the prior year's sizeable gain, world lentils output is seen contracting by 9% y/y in 2026/27, chiefly tied to a smaller Canadian harvest. With consumption only marginally higher, also taking account of heavy carry-ins, global end-season inventories are expected to expand solidly, including in key exporters. Trade volumes are predicted little-changed y/y, at 5.3m t, underpinned by Asian demand. (see chart) MARKET SUMMARY Some earlier advances in world grains and oilseeds export quotations were unwound in recent weeks, with the IGC GOI down by a net 4%. (see chart) (see chart) Mainly because of softer North American export quotations, the IGC GOI wheat sub-Index dropped by 5%. US fob values were pressed by disappointing export progress, currency movements and spillover from maize. (see chart) The IGC GOI maize sub-Index slumped by 7%, weighed predominantly by supply side considerations, including two bearishly perceived USDA reports. (see chart) With tight nearby availabilities lending price support in several markets, the IGC GOI rice sub-Index rose by 2% m/m, up by 21% compared to a year earlier. (see chart) The IGC GOI soyabeans sub-Index eased by 3%. Light pressure stemmed from some disappointment about the outcome of US-China bilateral talks, seasonal factors and a good start to the Brazilian planting season. The European markets broadly ended mixed but tracked sideways week-on-week. The mix in market momentum last week was due to the latest USDA World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates, geopolitics, and global demand. While the market looks generally well supplied globally, uncertainty around geopolitics continues to cause uncertainty in global price sentiment. The main driver of market pressure was the USDA unexpectedly raising its US maize production estimate to 407.3 Mt, after increases to national yields. Further to that, beginning stocks increased following the September Grain Stocks report. Although demand was revised higher, the increase in supply was larger, pushing 2026/27 US ending stocks up to 47 Mt. The US is now expected to produce the second-largest maize crop on record. This pressured US maize futures, which traded down by their daily limit on Friday. The trade had expected cuts to this crop after summer heat and ongoing wet harvests. Another driver of market sentiment has been US weather. In the last seven days, US rains have been minimal, so progress should be positive in the latest USDA crop progress report tomorrow evening. However, with rain forecast in the coming week, a slowdown in field work could be a watchpoint for markets. Disruptions in Black Sea exports continue to underpin prices in Europe. With minimal progress towards a complete ceasefire, the Ukrainian farm minister is seeking more alternative routes in Germany and the Baltics to increase their trade capacity. Current alternatives leave Ukrainian grain uncompetitive in the global market, due to increased logistical costs. Analysis of risks, weather focus and price outlook. European wheat starts the 2026/27 winter season with sharp regional contrasts: timely sowing and good emergence in Germany, Poland and Ukraine versus drought-delayed crops in Central Europe and waterlogged, undersown fields in the Baltics. This pattern raises medium‑term production risk even as flat prices remain soft. Wheat markets are currently balancing comfortable global supplies and weak flat prices with a more weather‑sensitive outlook for the 2027 European crop. Futures on Euronext and CBOT have eased over the past week, reflecting ample export competition, including aggressive Black Sea offers. Yet the new EU crop is entering winter with clear vulnerabilities: dryness in Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary, and major sowing delays in the Baltics, while France lags slightly but has recently benefited from rain. For now, these issues translate into a modest risk premium in deferred contracts rather than an outright bull market. Prices Euronext milling wheat futures for Dec-26 are trading around the low €230s/t, having slipped by roughly 4% over the last five sessions, while the Sep-27 contract – the first 2027‑crop month – trades at a discount near the mid‑€220s/t, indicating only a limited weather risk premium so far. referenceContext.quote: Indian Wheat Turns Mixed as Government Auctions Meet Festive Demand CMB CMB News Editorial Editorial Desk October 27, 2026 Indian wheat prices trade mixed as early OMSS auctions, flour-mill demand and ample stocks balance regional tightness. Brief outlook and price indications. Indian wheat prices are trading in a mixed pattern as government auction volumes and varying flour-mill demand pull local markets in different directions, while other staples such as basmati rice weaken on softer export interest. Festive restocking is supporting selected wheat centres, but overall supply from public stocks remains sufficient to prevent a broad-based rally. Indian wholesale grain trade currently reflects a two-speed market. Wheat and chana are firmer in selected centres on improved buying and tighter spot availability, whereas basmati rice and several pulses face weaker quotations amid subdued export and domestic demand. Early-season government wheat auctions and solid flour-mill interest ahead of Diwali are underpinning prices where local pipelines had emptied, but ample state-held stocks and ongoing e-auctions limit upside. This leaves the near-term outlook one of range-bound, locally differentiated wheat pricing rather than a uniform bull run across India. Prices In Indian wholesale markets, wheat prices are described as mixed rather than clearly trending, with direction largely determined by local access to government auction grain and the intensity of flour-mill purchasing. Where auction volumes are modest versus mill demand, quotations have firmed; in other centres, steady or easier levels persist as supplies remain comfortable. Internationally, recent data in EUR terms show relatively stable export quotations. India’s corn market is firm as weak kharif yields, strong ethanol and feed demand and rising transport costs tighten supplies despite new crop arrivals.
Prices
Indian corn prices have moved noticeably higher in recent weeks as tightening fundamentals overshadow the typical harvest-pressure effect from new arrivals. Traders in producing states report that fresh kharif lots are being offered at elevated levels, with market participants expecting quotations to rise by roughly US$2.12 per quintal in the near term if supply constraints continue.
Quality differentials are widening: better-quality corn from Bihar is attracting higher prices than new-crop supplies from parts of central India, where grain size and test weight are reportedly below normal. Internationally, benchmark CBOT corn futures have softened over the last month, adding a modestly bearish external signal, but this has so far done little to cool India’s predominantly domestic-driven rally.

Supply & Demand
New kharif corn arrivals have begun in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and other producers, but reports of reduced domestic production and smaller grain size suggest that total usable supply may be significantly tighter than last year. The delayed and uneven monsoon has already pushed back harvest calendars in several maize belts, implying a more staggered and potentially prolonged arrival window this season.
On the demand side, ethanol manufacturers remain a major structural driver, requiring consistently large volumes of corn alongside starch and feed producers. Recent policy signals around limiting sugar diversion to ethanol could reinforce the role of grains such as corn in upcoming blending tenders, sustaining demand even as overall ethanol pathways are rebalanced. At the same time, poultry and livestock feed buyers face higher input costs and are competing aggressively for spot supplies, particularly for good-quality lots.
Fundamentals & Weather
Fundamentals are tightening from both sides: lower yields and quality issues are limiting marketable supply, while firm industrial and feed demand are absorbing arrivals relatively quickly. Transportation costs have risen due to higher fuel prices, widening regional basis levels and discouraging long-distance movements from surplus to deficit zones.
Weather remains a key uncertainty for the tail end of the kharif harvest and early storage period. Earlier rainfall deficits and localized heat stress have already reduced yield potential across parts of central India, and any additional unseasonal rain during harvest could further damage grain quality or delay drying. With global futures markets relatively soft but domestic cash markets firm, India’s corn balance sheet is increasingly decoupled from international benchmarks and driven by internal supply-demand frictions.
Outlook & Trading Ideas
Market participants broadly expect corn prices in India to remain supported in the near term, with traders flagging scope for quotations to increase by around US$2.12 per quintal if supply stays constrained. The interaction between new-crop arrivals, ethanol procurement, and feed demand will determine whether the market stabilizes later in the season or transitions into a more pronounced bull phase.
For ethanol and starch manufacturers: Lock in physical supply where possible but avoid overcommitting at current elevated levels until clarity emerges on government ethanol blending and feedstock allocations.
For traders/exporters: Domestic fundamentals point to a firmer basis; export opportunities may be limited unless international values rally or Indian prices correct on larger-than-expected arrivals.
India (FOB New Delhi, starch corn): Stable to slightly firmer over the next three days as industrial demand stays strong and quality concerns linger.
EU (FOB Paris / EXW Germany feed corn): Slightly softer bias amid comfortable local supplies and weaker CBOT futures, though moves likely limited in the very short term.
Black Sea (Ukraine FOB/CPT): Mostly steady with a mild downward tilt, reflecting recent price easing and competitive export offers.

Corn prices in Germany, Euronext and CBOT continue to ease under fast US harvest, weak export sales and sharply lower Ukrainian shipments. Concise outlook.
Prices
Euronext corn futures ended the week mixed but with a clear downward bias. The March 2027 contract closed unchanged on Friday at 265.25 EUR/t, yet posted a weekly loss of 6.00 EUR or 2.2% from 271.25 EUR/t the previous Friday, mirroring weaker sentiment in global markets.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, front-month December corn settled at 456.0 US cents/bu (around 160 EUR/t), down 4.5 cents on the day and 18.25 cents or 3.8% on the week, as fresh harvest supplies hit the pipeline and speculative longs liquidated.
German cash prices continued to decline in tandem with futures. In Südoldenburg, corn was traded at 276 EUR/t on Friday, 6 EUR below Thursday and 13 EUR or 4.5% lower than a week earlier, underlining ample nearby availability and limited nearby demand.

CBOT Dec 2026 futures 456.0 USc/bu -18.25 USc (-3.8%)
Germany (Südoldenburg) Corn, cash 276 EUR/t -13 EUR (-4.5%)
Supply & Demand
US supply is the dominant bearish factor. A fast-paced harvest has boosted physical availability across the Corn Belt, and recent USDA Crop Progress data confirm that fieldwork is advancing quickly thanks to mostly dry conditions. Short-term forecasts point to scattered rains this week that may temporarily slow harvest, but not enough to meaningfully tighten supply.
US export demand remains underwhelming. According to the latest USDA export data, total US corn sales so far in the marketing year stand at around 22.1 million tonnes, 34% below last year, with only 26% of USDA’s full-season export projection on the books compared with a five-year average pace of about 37%. At the same time, shipments of 9.54 million tonnes slightly exceed last year and are ahead of the average pace, at 11% of the season versus an 8% norm, indicating that execution rather than new buying is carrying the program so far.
Ukraine is a notable wild card on the world balance sheet. Exports from 1 to 20 October reached only 200,000 tonnes of corn, far below prior years when monthly corn shipments often approached 2 million tonnes. Total grain exports this month are about 972,000 tonnes, roughly 40% less than a year ago, reflecting both logistical constraints and possibly farmers’ reluctance to sell at current prices.
In contrast, European domestic availability looks comfortable. Euronext futures structure and German cash price weakness point to good new-crop supply and active farmer selling. Current product quotations show EU-origin yellow corn FOB Paris at 0.28 EUR/kg and German feed corn EXW Drentwede at 0.282 EUR/kg, while Ukrainian FOB and inland values have eased in recent days, underscoring competitive Black Sea offers even at reduced export volumes.
The latest weekly report from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission shows that financial investors have sharply reduced their net long position in CBOT corn. As of 20 October, net longs fell by 84,620 contracts to 146,257, with new shorts added and existing longs liquidated, signalling waning confidence in a near-term price recovery.
USDA export data underscore the sluggish demand side. External analysis of the same figures highlights that accumulated US corn export commitments are roughly one-third below last year, and while recent weekly sales have occasionally surprised to the upside, they remain insufficient to offset the drag from large new-crop supplies and still-ample global stocks.
Weather & Harvest Outlook
Weather has so far been broadly supportive for the US harvest. A stretch of dry conditions allowed for rapid progress across much of the Corn Belt, which is reflected in rising on-farm stocks and pressure on basis levels. Forecasts now point to some rain episodes in the coming days that could temporarily slow fieldwork in parts of the Midwest but are unlikely to reverse the bearish impact of abundant new-crop supply.
In Europe, the harvest is largely advanced and recent weather poses limited risk to yields or quality. In Ukraine, drier windows have allowed harvest to move forward, and despite infrastructure challenges, the physical flow of corn to ports and border crossings is set to increase in the coming weeks, adding to regional supply even if export volumes remain well below historical norms.
Trading Outlook (Next 1–2 Weeks)
Producers (EU & US): Consider scaling in additional hedges on rallies via futures or options, as the combination of rapid US harvest and weak export demand argues for continued downside or sideways trade in the short term.
Feed buyers in the EU: Use current price weakness to extend coverage modestly into Q1–Q2 2027, particularly in Germany and neighbouring markets where cash values have eased significantly.
Importers: Monitor Ukrainian and Black Sea offers closely. Even at reduced export volumes, current FOB and CPT prices from Odesa are competitive and may offer attractive alternatives to US or EU-origin corn.
3-Day Price Indication
Euronext Corn (Mar 2027): Slightly bearish to sideways, with harvest and Black Sea competition limiting rebounds above recent highs.
CBOT Corn (Dec 2026): Bias lower to sideways as US harvest advances; limited support expected unless export sales or weather surprise on the bullish side.
German Cash Corn (Südoldenburg): Mild further downside possible as local supply builds, though short-term farmer selling fatigue could flatten the curve later in the week.

referenceContext.quote: BriefsFinance BriefsFinance ✕ Free Newsletter NEWS / Global ScoopMalaysia's Palm Oil Output Poised for October Record, With 2027 Constraints on the HorizonAndre SavagePublished Oct 19, 2026 Share: Summary: Malaysia's growers say October could set a new monthly production high. Full-year output is likely to meet or surpass the 20.28 million tons peak from 2025, per the industry group's chief. Labor shortages and the lagged impact of El Niño threaten supplies in 2027. What just happened Malaysia's top growers say October is shaping up to be the biggest production month ever. The strength follows an all-time monthly high in September, when output jumped 16% from August to 2.12 million tons, lifting nationwide inventories 25% to 3.51 million tons. Last October's mark for the month was 2.04 million tons. Roslin Azmy Hassan, who heads the Malaysian Palm Oil Association, expects 2026 production to match or exceed the prior full-year record of 20.28 million tons set in 2025. He tied the recent lift in supply to replanted areas maturing since June, with younger palms yielding more fruit. As he put it, "The better planting material bears more fruit compared with the material used 25 years ago." He added that after an October peak, output may taper in November and December, then run into tighter conditions in 2027 due to a lingering labor shortfall and the delayed hit from El Niño. Why prices and stocks moved Palm oil is up 18% in 2026 even as Malaysia - the world's No. 2 grower - has seen inventories climb to a record. Prices have been propelled by pricier global energy linked to conflict in the Middle East, Indonesia expanding its biodiesel mandate, and expectations that El Niño will curb production ahead. Benchmark futures touched 5,049 ringgit in mid September, the highest intraday level since December 2024. On Monday in Kuala Lumpur, prices briefly climbed 1.1% to 4,821 ringgit per ton before easing to 4,779 ringgit as of 4:15 p.m. local time. The supply surge since June has been helped by replanted, higher yielding estates coming into their stride, which has padded both output and stockpiles even as prices climbed. Palm oil remains a staple ingredient in foods and biofuels, so both energy markets and biofuel policy feed into demand. When market signals keep changing, stay steady with our free Market Briefs newsletter that sums it up in five minutes The risk ahead Roslin warned that today's big harvest is masking structural strain. Malaysia is short roughly 18,000 harvesters, which could leave about 8.6 million tons of fresh fruit bunches on the trees and translate into around 8 billion ringgit in lost revenue, or $1.96 billion. Planters have been pulling staff from maintenance to keep harvesting going, but that quick fix disrupts essentials like fertilizer application and general upkeep. The workforce gap has been hard to close. Plantations lean heavily on foreign labor, and rebuilding headcount after pandemic border curbs has been held back by quotas and tighter controls. That labor issue could combine with the delayed effects of El Niño to hit output next year, with the weather impact expected to show up more clearly in the second half of 2027. "If you don't bring in new workers next year, then you'll see the impact on production," Roslin said. What this means for your portfolio Near term, Malaysia's bumper crop supports higher inventories alongside firm prices. Looking out, the setup shifts: costs have climbed over recent years to roughly 2,600 to 3,000 ringgit per ton, and with a planned minimum wage hike next year, plantation margins face additional pressure, which may prompt companies to pare back other expenditures. Add in the potential 2027 supply drag from a thinner workforce and a lagged El Niño, and price volatility stays on the table for palm oil and related consumer goods and biofuel plays. MPOB said crude palm oil (CPO) stocks increased 31.88%, or 522,905 tonnes, to 2.16 million tonnes in September from 1.64 million tonnes in August. “Processed palm oil stockpile jumped 14.33 %, or 168,930 tonnes, to 1.34 million tonnes from 1.17 million tonnes in August,” it said in its Malaysian Palm Oil Industry, August 2026, performance report. On production, MPOB said CPO output rose 16.48%, or 299,451 tonnes, to 2.11 million tonnes in September. This compared to 1.81 million tonnes a month earlier, while palm kernel output gained 18.16% month-on-month to 508,392 tonnes from 430,599 tonnes. Crude palm kernel oil production increased 4.91% to 209,381 tonnes from August, while palm kernel cake output climbed 7.81 % to 232,696 tonnes. MPOB said palm oil exports, however, declined 12.13% in September 2026 to 1.22 million tonnes from a month earlier. Palm kernel oil exports fell 34.09% to 74,364 tonnes from a month ago. Palm kernel cake exports fell by 3.99% to 204,687 tonnes. Meanwhile, oleochemical exports increased 2.62% to 239,723 tonnes from August, while biodiesel exports fell 91.69% to 2,930 tonnes from last month. MPOB reported zero CPO imports in September. Processed palm oil inched up 3.49% to 51,252 tonnes from 49,524 tonnes, while palm oil leaped 17.25% to 58,064 tonnes from the preceding month. inputs.rawTitle: Indian Corn Market Tightens as Kharif Arrivals Fail to Ease Supply Stress
inputs.rawSnippet:
India’s corn market is firm as weak kharif yields, strong ethanol and feed demand and rising transport costs tighten supplies despite new crop arrivals.
Prices
Indian corn prices have moved noticeably higher in recent weeks as tightening fundamentals overshadow the typical harvest-pressure effect from new arrivals. Traders in producing states report that fresh kharif lots are being offered at elevated levels, with market participants expecting quotations to rise by roughly US$2.12 per quintal in the near term if supply constraints continue.
Quality differentials are widening: better-quality corn from Bihar is attracting higher prices than new-crop supplies from parts of central India, where grain size and test weight are reportedly below normal. Internationally, benchmark CBOT corn futures have softened over the last month, adding a modestly bearish external signal, but this has so far done little to cool India’s predominantly domestic-driven rally.

Supply & Demand
New kharif corn arrivals have begun in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and other producers, but reports of reduced domestic production and smaller grain size suggest that total usable supply may be significantly tighter than last year. The delayed and uneven monsoon has already pushed back harvest calendars in several maize belts, implying a more staggered and potentially prolonged arrival window this season.
On the demand side, ethanol manufacturers remain a major structural driver, requiring consistently large volumes of corn alongside starch and feed producers. Recent policy signals around limiting sugar diversion to ethanol could reinforce the role of grains such as corn in upcoming blending tenders, sustaining demand even as overall ethanol pathways are rebalanced. At the same time, poultry and livestock feed buyers face higher input costs and are competing aggressively for spot supplies, particularly for good-quality lots.
Fundamentals & Weather
Fundamentals are tightening from both sides: lower yields and quality issues are limiting marketable supply, while firm industrial and feed demand are absorbing arrivals relatively quickly. Transportation costs have risen due to higher fuel prices, widening regional basis levels and discouraging long-distance movements from surplus to deficit zones.
Weather remains a key uncertainty for the tail end of the kharif harvest and early storage period. Earlier rainfall deficits and localized heat stress have already reduced yield potential across parts of central India, and any additional unseasonal rain during harvest could further damage grain quality or delay drying. With global futures markets relatively soft but domestic cash markets firm, India’s corn balance sheet is increasingly decoupled from international benchmarks and driven by internal supply-demand frictions.
Outlook & Trading Ideas
Market participants broadly expect corn prices in India to remain supported in the near term, with traders flagging scope for quotations to increase by around US$2.12 per quintal if supply stays constrained. The interaction between new-crop arrivals, ethanol procurement, and feed demand will determine whether the market stabilizes later in the season or transitions into a more pronounced bull phase.
For ethanol and starch manufacturers: Lock in physical supply where possible but avoid overcommitting at current elevated levels until clarity emerges on government ethanol blending and feedstock allocations.
For traders/exporters: Domestic fundamentals point to a firmer basis; export opportunities may be limited unless international values rally or Indian prices correct on larger-than-expected arrivals.

inputs.rawTitle: EU Corn Harvest Shock: Regional Losses Tighten Balance, Black Sea Caps Prices
inputs.rawSnippet:
EU corn yields drop 9% below average in 2026, with heavy losses in Hungary, France and Germany, while strong Black Sea supply caps price upside.
Prices
Euronext corn futures in Paris have firmed but remain far from panic levels, reflecting tighter EU fundamentals but ample wider‑region supply. Nearby Euronext corn settled around the high €270s per tonne on 23 October 2026, with only modest gains so far despite the deep yield cuts in several member states.
Physical quotations in the EU and Black Sea show a similar picture of underpinned but not spiking prices. Recent offers include corn (yellow, non‑organic, origin France) at EUR 0.28/kg FOB Paris and German feed‑grade corn at EUR 0.275/kg EXW Drentwede, both little changed over the past week. Ukrainian corn values have softened: FOB Odesa fell from EUR 0.139/kg to 0.134/kg between 16 and 23 October, while FCA Odesa feed corn eased from EUR 0.17/kg to 0.16/kg over roughly the same period, underscoring pressure from new‑crop arrivals.
Supply & Demand Landscape
The European Commission’s latest assessment puts average EU grain maize yields for 2026 at 6.42 t/ha, around 9% below the five‑year mean and 10% below last season. This confirms a clear tightening of the EU corn balance, especially in net‑exporting areas of Central and Western Europe.
Germany’s crop is notably hit as well. Average grain maize yields are seen at 7.88 t/ha, about 19% below the five‑year norm, following prolonged dryness and heat in southern and western regions. Premature ripening, poor cob development and the early conversion of grain maize into silage to cover forage shortages will all curtail grain availability, tightening local feed markets and likely raising internal German and Benelux demand for imports or intra‑EU inflows.
By contrast, South‑East Europe and parts of the Black Sea region provide important relief. Bulgaria is expected to reach about 5.76 t/ha, 34% above its five‑year average, and Romania 4.64 t/ha, 15% higher than normal. Outside the EU, Ukraine’s yield forecast of 7.40 t/ha sits roughly 4% above its own five‑year mean, while Turkey’s crop is close to its long‑term level at 9.67 t/ha after a modest weather‑driven downgrade. This regional split means Western Europe leans increasingly on supplies from the East.
In Ukraine, the ongoing corn harvest and strong on‑farm stocks have kept export prices under pressure despite elevated logistics costs and continuing war‑related risks. New‑crop supply continues to weigh on bids at Black Sea and Danube ports, where dollar‑denominated FOB quotes have edged lower over the past week, in line with the EUR‑based offers around Odesa.
This relative weakness in Ukrainian pricing (and similar competitiveness in other Black Sea origins) is a key brake on EU corn futures despite the sharp yield shock in Hungary, France, Austria and Germany. Import demand from North Africa and the Middle East can still be largely covered by Black Sea origins, while South‑Eastern EU member states with above‑average crops may even retain some exportable surplus. As a result, physical premiums in deficit Western regions are more likely to widen versus futures and versus Eastern origins, rather than futures themselves entering a runaway rally.
Weather & Short‑Term Outlook
With the 2026 EU corn crop largely determined, near‑term weather plays a limited role for yields but remains important for harvest pace and grain quality. Current forecasts for the next 7–10 days indicate mostly dry to slightly showery conditions across much of Central and Western Europe, which should support field work and reduce risks of late‑season disease or lodging; soil moisture deficits, however, remain severe in parts of Hungary and southern Germany, underlining structural vulnerability going into the 2027 season.
In the Black Sea zone, milder and relatively stable weather is expected to favour Ukrainian and Romanian harvest progress and logistics, reinforcing the near‑term availability of exportable corn. Any sudden disruptions to shipping channels or a shift to wetter, more disruptive patterns during the final harvest stages would be the main weather‑related bullish risks from here.
Trading & Procurement Outlook
Feed buyers in Western and Central EU: Consider increasing coverage for Q4 2026–Q1 2027 while basis levels are still manageable. Local deficits in Germany, France and Hungary argue for a gradual scale‑in of purchases, particularly from South‑Eastern EU and Black Sea origins.
Producers in surplus regions (Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine): The combination of weak flat prices and tight EU fundamentals favours flexible selling strategies. Hedge a portion of expected exports against Euronext, but retain some upside exposure in case of logistics shocks or further yield downgrades in Western Europe.
Traders and originators: Monitor basis differentials between Euronext futures, Western EU physical markets and Black Sea offers. The structural yield shortfall in Hungary, France and Germany should widen East‑West spreads and create cross‑border arbitrage opportunities, particularly via Danube and Adriatic routes.
Euronext corn (Paris): Bias mildly firm, with downside limited by poor EU yields but capped by competitive Black Sea offers.
Western EU physical markets (France, Germany): Stable to slightly firmer premiums over futures expected as local feed users secure additional coverage.
Black Sea (Ukraine, Romania): Corn export prices likely to remain under slight pressure from ongoing harvest and strong nearby availability, barring any renewed escalation in logistical risks.

inputs.rawTitle: Corn under Harvest Pressure as EU and US Prices Extend Losses
inputs.rawSnippet:
Corn prices in Germany, Euronext and CBOT continue to ease under fast US harvest, weak export sales and sharply lower Ukrainian shipments. Concise outlook.
Prices
Euronext corn futures ended the week mixed but with a clear downward bias. The March 2027 contract closed unchanged on Friday at 265.25 EUR/t, yet posted a weekly loss of 6.00 EUR or 2.2% from 271.25 EUR/t the previous Friday, mirroring weaker sentiment in global markets.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, front-month December corn settled at 456.0 US cents/bu (around 160 EUR/t), down 4.5 cents on the day and 18.25 cents or 3.8% on the week, as fresh harvest supplies hit the pipeline and speculative longs liquidated.
German cash prices continued to decline in tandem with futures. In Südoldenburg, corn was traded at 276 EUR/t on Friday, 6 EUR below Thursday and 13 EUR or 4.5% lower than a week earlier, underlining ample nearby availability and limited nearby demand.

Supply & Demand
US supply is the dominant bearish factor. A fast-paced harvest has boosted physical availability across the Corn Belt, and recent USDA Crop Progress data confirm that fieldwork is advancing quickly thanks to mostly dry conditions. Short-term forecasts point to scattered rains this week that may temporarily slow harvest, but not enough to meaningfully tighten supply.
US export demand remains underwhelming. According to the latest USDA export data, total US corn sales so far in the marketing year stand at around 22.1 million tonnes, 34% below last year, with only 26% of USDA’s full-season export projection on the books compared with a five-year average pace of about 37%. At the same time, shipments of 9.54 million tonnes slightly exceed last year and are ahead of the average pace, at 11% of the season versus an 8% norm, indicating that execution rather than new buying is carrying the program so far.
Ukraine is a notable wild card on the world balance sheet. Exports from 1 to 20 October reached only 200,000 tonnes of corn, far below prior years when monthly corn shipments often approached 2 million tonnes. Total grain exports this month are about 972,000 tonnes, roughly 40% less than a year ago, reflecting both logistical constraints and possibly farmers’ reluctance to sell at current prices.
In contrast, European domestic availability looks comfortable. Euronext futures structure and German cash price weakness point to good new-crop supply and active farmer selling. Current product quotations show EU-origin yellow corn FOB Paris at 0.28 EUR/kg and German feed corn EXW Drentwede at 0.282 EUR/kg, while Ukrainian FOB and inland values have eased in recent days, underscoring competitive Black Sea offers even at reduced export volumes.
The latest weekly report from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission shows that financial investors have sharply reduced their net long position in CBOT corn. As of 20 October, net longs fell by 84,620 contracts to 146,257, with new shorts added and existing longs liquidated, signalling waning confidence in a near-term price recovery.
USDA export data underscore the sluggish demand side. External analysis of the same figures highlights that accumulated US corn export commitments are roughly one-third below last year, and while recent weekly sales have occasionally surprised to the upside, they remain insufficient to offset the drag from large new-crop supplies and still-ample global stocks.
Weather & Harvest Outlook
Weather has so far been broadly supportive for the US harvest. A stretch of dry conditions allowed for rapid progress across much of the Corn Belt, which is reflected in rising on-farm stocks and pressure on basis levels. Forecasts now point to some rain episodes in the coming days that could temporarily slow fieldwork in parts of the Midwest but are unlikely to reverse the bearish impact of abundant new-crop supply.
In Europe, the harvest is largely advanced and recent weather poses limited risk to yields or quality. In Ukraine, drier windows have allowed harvest to move forward, and despite infrastructure challenges, the physical flow of corn to ports and border crossings is set to increase in the coming weeks, adding to regional supply even if export volumes remain well below historical norms.
Trading Outlook (Next 1–2 Weeks)
Producers (EU & US): Consider scaling in additional hedges on rallies via futures or options, as the combination of rapid US harvest and weak export demand argues for continued downside or sideways trade in the short term.
Feed buyers in the EU: Use current price weakness to extend coverage modestly into Q1–Q2 2027, particularly in Germany and neighbouring markets where cash values have eased significantly.
Importers: Monitor Ukrainian and Black Sea offers closely. Even at reduced export volumes, current FOB and CPT prices from Odesa are competitive and may offer attractive alternatives to US or EU-origin corn.
3-Day Price Indication
Euronext Corn (Mar 2027): Slightly bearish to sideways, with harvest and Black Sea competition limiting rebounds above recent highs.
CBOT Corn (Dec 2026): Bias lower to sideways as US harvest advances; limited support expected unless export sales or weather surprise on the bullish side.
German Cash Corn (Südoldenburg): Mild further downside possible as local supply builds, though short-term farmer selling fatigue could flatten the curve later in the week.

inputs.rawTitle: Australian regulators consider two GM wheat lines
inputs.rawSnippet: Australian regulators consider two GM wheat lines Credit: ©MAECHING - STOCK.ADOBE.COM Oct 22, 2026 By John Reidy Add as a preferred source on Google CANBERRA, AUSTRALIA — Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) has opened a public comment period on an application to permit the sale and use of food derived from a pair of genetically modified (GM) wheat lines developed by the University of Melbourne. GM wheat lines containing an event called UM-12115T-1 have been modified to contain a gene from rice, which results in higher levels of nicotianamine, FSANZ said. Nicotianamine is a naturally occurring compound that helps plants absorb and distribute minerals such as iron and zinc. The GM wheat is intended primarily for use as animal feed, although if approved it also may enter the human food supply through food processing and grain supply chains, FSANZ said. The University of Melbourne also is seeking approval for commercial cultivation of these wheat lines in Australia through a separate assessment by the Office of the Gene Technology Regulator. The GM wheat had been previously grown in field trials in Australia. The university said a primary reason for seeking regulatory approval at this stage is the need to cultivate UM-12115T-1 over substantially larger areas to support research, market development and pre-commercial validation activities. “Expanded cultivation is required to generate the grain volumes necessary to undertake efficacy, operational and value-chain studies at commercially meaningful scale, including larger animal feeding trials and broader assessment of the line’s agronomic, nutritional and market potential,” the university said. FSANZ said its safety assessment focused on human food safety and nutrition and found no public health or safety concerns with food derived from GM wheat lines containing event UM-12115T-1. “It is as safe as food from conventional wheat varieties,” the agency said. FSANZ said it will consider all feedback received through the submission process by Dec. 1 before deciding on whether to approve the application. inputs.rawTitle: Crude palm oil prices in Malaysia to stay above $1,128/t in November — MPOC
inputs.rawSnippet: Home Agricultural market news Crude palm oil prices in Malaysia to stay above $1,128/t in November — MPOC 12:56, 22 October 2026 Source: Brecorder Crude palm oil prices in Malaysia are expected to remain above MYR 4,600 ($1,128) per ton in November 2026, supported by stronger export demand, sustained biodiesel consumption and a seasonal decline in production. The forecast was released by the Malaysian Palm Oil Council (MPOC). According to the council, these factors are expected to support crude palm oil prices through the end of the year. One of the main factors supporting prices will be an expected decline in Malaysian palm oil inventories. Due to a seasonal slowdown in production, stocks are projected to decrease gradually from November 2026 through February 2027. MPOC believes this trend will provide further support to the market in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, the decline in exports recorded in September is considered temporary, with shipments expected to recover significantly during October–December. Additional market support could come from increased purchases by India and China, two of the world’s largest vegetable oil consumers. According to MPOC, these countries may increase palm oil imports in the coming months due to expected supply constraints for sunflower oil and soybean oil. This could intensify competition for Malaysian supplies and support export prices amid the seasonal production decline. Demand from the biofuel sector also remains an important factor. Elevated energy prices make vegetable oils more attractive for biodiesel production and encourage higher biodiesel blending rates. Indonesia has a particularly significant impact on the market, as its expanding biodiesel programs support domestic palm oil consumption. MPOC expects sustained high energy prices to contribute to further growth in demand for this feedstock. However, analysts also warn of risks to further price gains. The main downside factors include lower energy prices, which could weaken biodiesel demand, and weaker-than-expected vegetable oil consumption in the food industry. Inflation and economic uncertainty may also limit importers’ purchasing activity. As a result, the outlook for crude palm oil prices in late 2026 will depend on the balance between seasonal supply reductions, export demand and developments in global energy markets. inputs.rawTitle: India’s Soybean Squeeze Reshapes Trade Flows and Price Signals
inputs.rawSnippet:
India’s soybean shortage is pushing record imports, squeezing crushers and curbing soymeal exports, with Brazil-US weather and El Niño adding risk.
Prices
Physical soybean indications highlight notable regional differentials. Indian soybeans (sortex clean, FOB New Delhi) are quoted at 0.89 EUR/kg FOB, well above U.S. Soybeans No. 2 at 0.58 EUR/kg FOB Washington D.C. and Ukrainian soybeans at 0.333 EUR/kg FOB Odesa. Chinese yellow soybeans stand at 0.74 EUR/kg FOB Beijing, with organic yellow at 0.85 EUR/kg FOB Beijing.
The firm Indian FOB structure reflects domestic supply tightness and strong internal demand, in contrast to more competitively priced Black Sea and U.S. origins, where futures recently eased as harvest advanced and November contracts slipped below key moving averages. This price gap underpins India’s surge in imports while capping the competitiveness of Indian soymeal on export markets.
Supply & Demand
India’s soybean trade pattern has shifted sharply as domestic supplies tightened. Between October 2025 and June 2026, soybean imports jumped to around 777,000 tonnes, up from roughly 2,000 tonnes a year earlier. Industry estimates now point toward import volumes for the 2025/26 oil year approaching 1 million tonnes, underlining the depth of the shortfall.
At the same time, soybean meal exports have declined as domestic availability narrowed and high raw bean costs made Indian product less competitive internationally. Processors are increasingly focused on imported bean availability and domestic crushing margins, while Indian poultry and aquaculture feed manufacturers continue to absorb a large share of soymeal, keeping internal demand structurally strong.
Globally, soybean fundamentals in late October 2026 are shaped by a two‑continent storyline. In the U.S., harvest is well advanced and has recently pressured Chicago futures, with prices testing multi‑week lows as yield prospects remain generally favorable despite earlier weather concerns. Meanwhile, strong Chinese buying interest in new‑crop U.S. supplies has limited downside, even as managed money weighs a reduction in long exposure.
In South America, Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean campaign is progressing under an emerging Super El Niño backdrop. Early planting in Mato Grosso and the Center‑West is constrained by irregular rainfall and patchy soil moisture, with rainfall totals still below ideal in parts of the state and forecasts closely watched for confirmation of a sustained rainy‑season onset. Argentina’s core zones are generally near to slightly above normal on moisture, but distribution remains uneven, adding another layer of yield risk heading into the main growing months.
Weather Outlook for Key Regions
Brazil (Mato Grosso & Center‑West): Recent 15‑ to 30‑day rainfall has been modestly below to near normal, with the next 15 days expected to bring incremental improvement in moisture, potentially accelerating planting if projected rains verify. However, El Niño increases the risk of continued spatially irregular showers, keeping emergence and early vegetative development under scrutiny.
Argentina: Core soybean areas such as Córdoba, Santa Fe and Buenos Aires show generally adequate but uneven precipitation, with some northern zones trending drier. Under a strong El Niño signal, the market will closely track whether forecasted above‑normal rains in parts of southern Brazil and Argentina materialize, as this could offset U.S. harvest pressure and re‑tighten new‑crop balances.
Trading Outlook (Next 1–3 Months)
Indian crushers & feed buyers: Consider selectively locking in imported volumes from U.S. or Black Sea origins while FOB differentials remain wide versus Indian prices, to protect crush margins and hedge against further domestic supply tightness.
Exporters of Indian soymeal: Focus on niche, value‑added or non‑GMO segments rather than volume business; current bean costs and high domestic demand limit price competitiveness in mainstream destinations.
International buyers (Asia & MENA): Use current U.S. harvest‑driven weakness to extend coverage into Q1 2027 but retain some flexibility, as South American weather – especially in Brazil’s Center‑West – could quickly reverse the soft tone if planting delays persist.

inputs.rawTitle: EU Soybean Yields Slide 15%: What It Means for Prices and Imports
inputs.rawSnippet:
EU soybean yields are forecast 15% below the 5‑year average in 2026. See how this impacts imports, prices and trading strategies in the global soy market.
Prices
These stable spot levels contrast with the significantly weaker EU yield outlook, implying that the regional production shortfall is currently being absorbed via international trade rather than through a sharp price spike. Basis and premiums for non-GM and nearby European origins, however, are likely to strengthen as local buyers secure supply.
Supply & Demand
The European Commission’s latest assessment projects the average EU soybean yield in 2026 at just 2.24 t/ha, 15% below the five‑year average and 17% below 2025. This confirms that the poor outlook flagged in September has largely been validated by ongoing harvest results.
Losses are particularly severe in France and Austria, where expected yields of 1.75 t/ha and 2.05 t/ha sit about 30% below their respective five‑year averages. Hungary (1.82 t/ha, −23%), Czechia (1.92 t/ha, −21%), Germany (2.40 t/ha, −17%) and Italy (2.65 t/ha, −17%) also face substantial underperformance versus normal levels. The result is a broad-based shortfall across many core EU soybean regions.
In contrast, Romania is projected at 2.34 t/ha, 19% above its five‑year average, and Poland at 2.53 t/ha, close to its long‑term norm. For Ukraine, the yield forecast stands at 2.35 t/ha, about 5% below the five‑year average, with harvest already well advanced. These mixed outcomes highlight widening intra‑European differences in soybean availability and underscore the likely need for higher net imports into deficit regions.
Fundamentals & Weather Drivers
The primary driver of the weak EU soybean performance has been persistent rainfall deficits combined with high temperatures and constrained water availability during key growth stages. This pattern was particularly damaging across much of Central and Western Europe, cutting yield potential even where area had expanded compared with previous seasons.
On the global side, speculative positioning has turned less aggressively bullish in recent weeks, with managed money long exposure easing while prices held near harvest lows, indicating a more balanced sentiment. Meanwhile, early-season rains in Brazil’s Center-West are supporting sowing progress in Mato Grosso and other core soybean states, though accumulation and distribution vary by region, implying some ongoing weather risk as planting advances.
For the coming 1–2 weeks, forecasts for key South American soybean belts point to generally adequate to above-normal precipitation in parts of Brazil’s Center-West, with more mixed patterns toward southern Brazil and northern Argentina. Overall, this reduces immediate concerns about a delayed planting campaign but keeps weather firmly in focus as the critical South American crop is established.
Forecast & Trading Outlook
With EU soybean yields locked in well below average, regional crushers and feed manufacturers are expected to lean more heavily on imports, particularly from the US, Brazil and Ukraine. However, given currently comfortable global balances and only moderate futures prices, the impact is more likely to be seen in regional basis and non-GM premiums than in a strong rally of the global flat price.
CBOT futures are likely to remain sensitive to South American weather headlines and any surprise shifts in Chinese demand or US export sales. In this environment, price action may oscillate within a relatively broad sideways band, with upward spikes possible if Brazil experiences planting or early-season crop stress, and downside risk tied to smooth South American development and continued strong export competition.
EU crushers and feed users: Consider bringing forward a portion of Q1–Q2 2027 coverage, particularly for non-GM and EU or nearby origins, to hedge against tightening regional availability and firmer basis.
Producers in surplus EU regions (e.g., Romania, Poland): Monitor regional basis levels closely; localized strength versus futures or imported parity could offer attractive selling opportunities as neighboring deficits deepen.

inputs.rawTitle: What happened to the US corn crop?
inputs.rawSnippet:
Then came this summer’s Pro Farmer Crop Tour event. Scouts on the seven-state tour projected corn production at 15.344 billion bushels, down 10% from the tour’s 2025 estimate and down 4.2% from the USDA’s Aug. 12 forecast of 16.013 billion bushels. The tour, which concluded Aug. 20, calculated corn yield at 173.2 bushels per acre, down from the USDA’s outlook of 180.7 bushels and the lowest yield since 2020.
These compounding factors helped boost the spot Chicago corn futures contract from a low of $4.02 per bushel on June 29 to a contract high of $5.18 per bushel on Sept. 2. It was a 29% jump that had occurred in just over two months, and the sharp rise ignited a bullish sentiment that drove speculative long positions to record lengths.
Broader factors also were lending support at the time. A surge in soybean futures ahead of the Sept. 14 US-China summit spilled over into the corn market. The International Grains Council lowered its 2026-27 global corn production forecast by 4 million tonnes, to 1.306 billion tonnes, citing crop losses from recent heat waves across Europe. Rising energy prices provided additional support, underpinning much of the agricultural commodity complex.
And then, after a scorching, drought-stressed summer, which had stoked fears of pollination problems and unfilled kernels, lengthy bands of rain descended upon the Corn Belt just as harvest got underway.
Yet there were cracks in the wall of bullish support, hinting at a different story for the corn crop.
While the Pro Farmer scout projections showed an overall decline in corn yield and production this year, their findings still pointed to a large crop, with production projected to rank as the third largest on record if realized.
“Last year was the gold standard,” said Brian Grete, senior grain and livestock analyst at Commstock Investments. “We had record production, record yield, and everyone wants to compare it to a year ago, but I think that’s kind of unfair to this year’s corn crop.”

Supply & Demand
Near-term supply expectations remain comfortable. Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean planting is advancing at a record or near-record pace, with estimates around one quarter of area already seeded by mid-October and ahead of last year. While some central regions report irregular rains and short dry spells, conditions so far are sufficient to maintain an above-trend production outlook.
On the demand side, meal and oil consumption remain supported by strong livestock feed requirements and resilient vegetable oil usage. However, macro headwinds and energy price volatility continue to cap upside in biodiesel-driven oil demand. The current complex-wide pullback therefore looks more like a repricing of weather and macro risk premia than the start of a structural demand contraction.
In China, the firm DCE board and stronger nearby contracts point to continued tightness in domestic old-crop availability, but the rally there has not yet translated into higher EUR-denominated FOB offers ex-Beijing. This may reflect local policy, currency and freight effects insulating domestic prices from immediate transmission into export indications.
Weather Snapshot
Weather remains the key near-term driver. In Brazil, forecasts continue to flag an El Niño-influenced pattern with phases of heat and irregular rainfall through November, raising intra-season volatility but not yet undermining the national soybean yield outlook. Recent updates highlight the risk of hot, dry spells in central regions interspersed with heavy storms in the south.
In Argentina, seasonal norms imply that most soybean regions receive the bulk of annual rainfall between October and March, providing a window for soil moisture recovery after earlier dryness. As of late October, there is no acute, widely reported weather shock, but markets are sensitive to any shift toward sustained dryness that could trim 2026/27 output.
30–90 Day Market Outlook & Trading Ideas
Producers: Consider using today’s still historically reasonable futures levels to incrementally hedge 2026/27 production, especially in regions exposed to El Niño-related yield risk. inputs.rawSnippet: PotatoEurope’s 2026 Potato Shortfall Tightens Supply but Prices Stay ManagedCMBCMB News EditorialEditorial DeskOctober 26, 2026EU potato yields in 2026 fall well below average, tightening raw potato and starch supply. Review key producing countries, price signals and a short‑term outlook.European potato supply in 2026 is set to be among the tightest of recent years as drought and heat drag EU yields about 8% below the five‑year average and 12% under 2025. This will underpin firm raw potato values and restrict downside for processing and starch markets, even as contracts and retail prices temper the full impact along the chain. The market is entering the storage season with clear regional contrasts. Germany and France face markedly reduced yields after prolonged dryness, Belgium reports smaller tuber sizes, and Austria is hit hardest with a quarter of its typical yield gone. By contrast, the Netherlands, Poland and Romania help cushion the overall EU balance with near‑average or above‑average results. Spot and futures markets in Northwest Europe are already signalling stress, while retail prices so far move more slowly. For derivative products like potato starch, stable quotations point to a firm but orderly adjustment phase rather than a price spike. Core 2026 harvest picture The Joint Research Centre’s latest assessment on 26 October 2026 pegs average EU potato yield at 34.2 t/ha, around 8% below the five‑year mean and 12% below last season. The worst losses are concentrated in Central and Western Europe, where a long dry, hot spell curtailed tuber growth and accelerated senescence. Austria stands out with only 24.3 t/ha, 25% under its long‑term average. Germany is estimated at 37.1 t/ha, 15% below its five‑year mean and 19% under 2025, while France at 35.5 t/ha is roughly 14% below average. Belgium’s 38.3 t/ha represents an 8% drop, with many fields reporting under‑sized tubers. The Netherlands is comparatively resilient at 41.5 t/ha, only 3% below average after late rain slightly improved the outlook compared with September. Further east, Poland is a notable bright spot at 31.5 t/ha, about 3% above its long‑term mean, and Romania is seen at 17.3 t/ha, up 13%. In the Baltics, heavy rainfall and water‑logged soils have delayed lifting, adding short‑term logistical tightness even where yields are not severely reduced. Overall, the EU harvest profile points to a materially smaller and more uneven crop, with exportable surpluses concentrated in just a few regions. Prices and spreads along the chain Processing potato spot markets in Northwest Europe have reacted quickly to the yield shock. Recent reports show Belgapom Fontane spot quotes around EUR 20 per 100 kg at the end of September, while PotatoNL ranged in the low‑ to high‑20s per 100 kg during the same period, significantly above many 2026 contract levels, which were signed 15–25% below last year’s prices. This creates a two‑tier market: tight free‑buy supply clears at elevated spot prices, while processors lean heavily on cheaper contracts signed pre‑drought. CNIPT’s week‑41 bulletin confirms that Northwest European processing quotes recently held broadly in the EUR 200–275/t band, underlining a firm but not disorderly market. Retail data across selected EU chains indicate that consumer prices for fresh potatoes have so far remained largely flat, with promotions doing most of the visible work as supermarkets absorb upstream tension. At the ingredient level, the European potato starch market is supported by tightening feedstock availability. Industry analysis notes that reduced processing potato supply has shifted sentiment to “stable to firm” going into October, with tighter raw material likely to cap downside in starch prices even as international trade flows remain relatively calm. Our own current quotation for conventional potato starch from Poland (Lodz, FCA) stands at 0.625 EUR/kg, unchanged across the last three updates in September and October 2026, signalling a steady but well‑supported market at the current level.
